headline: Hubbard freed. Witkoff calls Putin a humanitarian.
summary: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, a 74-year-old retired teacher sentenced to nearly seven years for allegedly fighting for Ukraine. Nothing was traded for him. US envoy Steve Witkoff thanked Putin in St Petersburg and called him a humanitarian. Some Republicans objected; Vance said the homecoming matters more than the word.

cover_question.q: Why did Russia let him go now?

cover_answer: Out of respect for Trump, Trump says. Nothing was traded.
table_question: Should you thank someone for fixing a thing they broke?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Stephen is an American teacher who is 74. Russia kept him in prison for more than four years, since before you started school. On Wednesday Russia let him go. An American helper flew there, said thank you, and now Stephen is on his way home to his family. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Four years as school years, a thank-you and a plane. Leave the war out.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script hands them four school years, a helper who said thank you and a plane home. The charge, the war and the row over the word stay out unless the child brings them in. Expect "why was he in prison?" Russia said he fought for Ukraine. America said that was wrong.

8-12.script: Stephen Hubbard, 74, was seized by Russian troops in Ukraine in 2022 and sentenced to nearly seven years. Russia freed him on Wednesday, no trade. The US envoy called Putin a humanitarian; some Republicans objected. A handshake after a foul: allowed, and the crowd judges it.
8-12.why: Seized, tried, freed, thanked. Then the handshake.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults keep their own rules, so the script runs the chain: seized, sentenced, freed, thanked. The handshake after a foul is the mechanism, allowed and judged by the crowd. Expect "why did Russia let him go now?" Trump says out of respect for him. Semafor: it costs Moscow little.

13-17.script: Is a man a humanitarian for freeing someone he should never have held? Witkoff said so; some in his own party objected. Days earlier Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. Second: Russia says it will talk next month; its aide calls Kyiv's ideas not very useful. Is the thank-you a price, and who pays it?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man is going home, and the envoy who got him out flattered the man who jailed him, days after the US eased sanctions on Russia. The script asks whether the thank-you is a price and who pays it, Hubbard or Ukraine. Expect "so was it a trade?" No swap, Trump says. The rest is argument.

5-7.a: Someone who helps people. The American helper called the Russian leader one for letting Stephen go. Lots of grown-ups disagreed.

8-12.q: Why did Russia let him go now?
8-12.a: Respect for Trump, Trump says. No trade. Semafor: it costs Moscow little.

8-12.q: Why are people cross about a thank-you?
8-12.a: Russia jailed him in the first place. Many found the word too kind for Putin.

13-17.q: Did Russia get something for him?
13-17.a: No swap, Trump says. Days earlier the US lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
Talks next month, Russia says, technical level only. I wouldn't count on it.
